statuses.label: Company trading posts
statuses.short: A business with forts, not a government.
statuses.definition: A chartered company rents or is granted a few coastal factories and warehouses. It trades, arms its own ships and hires soldiers, but it does not govern the country around it. Surat 1613, Fort St George 1639, Hudson Bay 1670.

statuses.label: Company rule
statuses.short: A private company collecting taxes and running courts.
statuses.definition: The same company now governs: it collects land revenue, keeps an army and appoints judges, under a charter from London and with no vote for anyone it rules. The East India Company ran Bengal this way from 1765 to 1858.

statuses.label: Proprietary colony
statuses.short: A colony owned by a person or a syndicate.
statuses.definition: The Crown grants the land and the right to govern it to an individual or a group, who then appoint the governor and pocket the quit-rents. Maryland (the Calverts), Pennsylvania (the Penns), Carolina (eight Lords Proprietors).

statuses.label: Representative government
statuses.short: An elected assembly, but a governor London appoints.
statuses.definition: Property-owning male settlers elect an assembly that votes taxes and makes local law. The governor is appointed in London, can veto anything and does not answer to the assembly. The normal arrangement in the American colonies before 1776.

statuses.label: Crown colony
statuses.short: Ruled directly from London through an appointed governor.
statuses.definition: A governor appointed by the Colonial Office rules with a nominated council. There is no elected majority and often no elected member at all. After 1865 this became the standard form wherever the population was not white.

statuses.label: Responsible government
statuses.short: Local ministers run domestic affairs; Britain keeps foreign policy.
statuses.definition: The governor must take the advice of ministers who command the local assembly. Britain still controls defence, foreign relations and the right to disallow laws. Canada from 1848, the Australian colonies from the 1850s, Southern Rhodesia from 1923.

statuses.label: Direct Crown rule
statuses.short: Governed from London with no local legislature at all.
statuses.definition: Rule by governor, resident or commissioner alone. Used for garrisons, penal settlements, tiny islands and places Britain did not intend to settle: Aden, Perim, Ascension under the Admiralty.

statuses.label: Protectorate
statuses.short: Not annexed, but Britain decides.
statuses.definition: Britain declares the territory under its protection without annexing it. Local rulers keep their titles; a British commissioner controls foreign policy, and in practice much else. Northern Nigeria, Uganda, Nyasaland, Bechuanaland.

statuses.label: Protected state
statuses.short: A real ruler with a British adviser he cannot ignore.
statuses.definition: The state keeps its own ruler, laws and courts and is not British territory. Britain runs its foreign relations and stations an adviser or political agent. Kuwait 1899, Bahrain, Qatar, the Trucial States, Brunei, the Malay sultanates.

statuses.label: Princely state
statuses.short: An Indian ruler under British paramountcy.
statuses.definition: One of the 565 states of India that were never British territory. The ruler governed internally; the Crown controlled defence and foreign affairs and could depose him. Hyderabad, Mysore, Kashmir, Travancore.

statuses.label: League of Nations mandate
statuses.short: A colony held on paper for the League of Nations.
statuses.definition: Territory taken from Germany or the Ottoman Empire in 1919 and administered by Britain under League supervision, with a duty to report annually and prepare it for self-rule. Iraq, Palestine, Transjordan, Tanganyika, part of Togoland and Cameroon.

statuses.label: UN trusteeship
statuses.short: The same thing after 1945, supervised by the United Nations.
statuses.definition: The mandates that survived the war became UN trust territories in 1946, with visiting missions and a duty to lead them to independence. Tanganyika, the Cameroons, Togoland, New Guinea, Nauru, Western Samoa.

statuses.label: Condominium
statuses.short: Two powers governing the same place at once.
statuses.definition: Joint sovereignty. The New Hebrides had two police forces, three legal systems and no shared language of government from 1906 to 1980; the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan flew two flags and was run by Britain alone.

statuses.label: Leased territory
statuses.short: Rented, with an expiry date.
statuses.definition: Sovereignty stays with the original state; Britain gets full administration for a fixed term. Weihaiwei 1898-1930, the New Territories of Hong Kong on a 99-year lease from 1898, which is why all of Hong Kong went back in 1997.

statuses.label: Military occupation
statuses.short: Held by the army, with the legal position unsettled.
statuses.definition: British forces administer territory they have taken but not annexed, usually in wartime. Havana 1762, Java 1811-16, Constantinople 1918-23, the Italian colonies 1941-51, the British Zone of Germany 1945-49.

statuses.label: Dominion
statuses.short: Self-governing, still under the Crown, independence unclear.
statuses.definition: A self-governing state within the Empire sharing the monarch. After the Balfour Declaration of 1926 and the Statute of Westminster of 1931 Britain could no longer legislate for one. There is no agreed date on which a dominion became independent, which is why this atlas shows ranges.

statuses.label: Associated state
statuses.short: Full internal self-government; Britain keeps defence and foreign policy.
statuses.definition: A halfway house used in the eastern Caribbean from 1967 and in the Cook Islands and Niue. The state could end the arrangement unilaterally, and all of them eventually did.

statuses.label: British Overseas Territory
statuses.short: What is left today: British, self-governing, small.
statuses.definition: Called colonies until 1981, dependent territories until 2002. Fourteen remain, with a combined population of about 270,000 and a governor who still holds reserve powers, as Turks and Caicos found in 2009 when London suspended its constitution.

statuses.label: Crown dependency
statuses.short: Not in the UK, not a colony, older than both.
statuses.definition: Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man are possessions of the Crown that were never part of the United Kingdom and never colonies. They make their own laws and set their own taxes; the UK handles defence.

statuses.label: Part of the United Kingdom
statuses.short: Inside the state itself, not the empire around it.
statuses.definition: England, Wales and Scotland, and Ireland from 1801 to 1922, sending MPs to Westminster. Ireland is in this atlas because the arguments, the laws and the men used to govern it were rehearsed there first.

statuses.label: Informal empire
statuses.short: No flag, but Britain sets the terms.
statuses.definition: Britain controls the trade, the debt, the navy in the harbour or the ruler’s advisers without owning the place. Argentina, Persia, Siam, China’s treaty ports, Egypt before 1882. Leaving these off the map makes the empire look far smaller than it was.

peak.note: Computed by tools/audit-timeline.js from this dataset, not copied from a book. The conventional figure is about 33.7 million km², roughly a quarter of the world’s land. Run `node tools/audit-timeline.js --check` to re-test it.

keyDates.label: Newfoundland claimed
keyDates.why: Humphrey Gilbert claims St John’s for Elizabeth I. Nothing sticks, but the claim is the one England keeps citing.

keyDates.label: East India Company chartered
keyDates.why: A trading monopoly that ends up governing 300 million people.

keyDates.label: Jamestown founded
keyDates.why: The first English settlement in America that survives.

keyDates.label: First enslaved Africans in Virginia
keyDates.why: About 20 people, sold from a privateer. The beginning of English slavery in North America.

keyDates.label: Jamaica taken from Spain
keyDates.why: Cromwell’s Western Design fails at Hispaniola, takes Jamaica by accident, and creates the largest slave colony in the British Caribbean.

keyDates.label: Hudson’s Bay Company chartered
keyDates.why: A charter over the whole Hudson Bay watershed: 3.9 million square kilometres granted by a king who had never seen it.

keyDates.label: Union of England and Scotland
keyDates.why: Scotland enters the empire as a partner, and Scots go on to run a disproportionate share of it.

keyDates.label: Plassey
keyDates.why: A rigged battle that hands the Company Bengal’s revenues and turns a trading firm into a state.

keyDates.label: Treaty of Paris
keyDates.why: Canada, Florida and the eastern Mississippi become British. The bill for the war becomes the American crisis.

keyDates.label: Royal Proclamation
keyDates.why: Bars settlement west of the Appalachians. A grievance in America; the foundation of Aboriginal title in Canadian law.

keyDates.label: American Declaration of Independence
keyDates.why: The claim, not the fact. Britain fights on for seven more years.

keyDates.label: Treaty of Paris
keyDates.why: Britain recognises the United States. The empire’s largest settler population is gone, and the empire grows anyway.

keyDates.label: First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove
keyDates.why: A penal colony on land occupied for tens of thousands of years and declared empty.

keyDates.label: Slave Trade Act
keyDates.why: The trade abolished; slavery itself continues for 27 more years.

keyDates.label: Slavery Abolition Act
keyDates.why: Frees about 800,000 people, pays their owners £20 million, and makes the freed work unpaid as "apprentices" until 1838.

keyDates.label: Aden taken
keyDates.why: A coaling station on the route to India. The first territory Queen Victoria’s forces annexed.

keyDates.label: Treaty of Waitangi
keyDates.why: Two texts that do not say the same thing, still argued in New Zealand courts.

keyDates.label: Treaty of Nanking
keyDates.why: Hong Kong ceded, five treaty ports opened. Informal empire in China begins with a war over opium.

keyDates.label: Indian Rebellion begins
keyDates.why: The Company’s army mutinies at Meerut; a year later the Company is abolished.

keyDates.label: Government of India Act
keyDates.why: The Crown takes over from the Company. India becomes an imperial state, not a business.

keyDates.label: Canada confederates
keyDates.why: The first dominion. The model every settler colony then asks for.

keyDates.label: Victoria proclaimed Empress of India
keyDates.why: Disraeli’s title, invented for a durbar, that fixes India at the centre of imperial self-image.

keyDates.label: Britain occupies Egypt
keyDates.why: A temporary occupation to protect bondholders and the canal. It lasts 74 years.

keyDates.label: Berlin Conference opens
keyDates.why: The rules for partitioning Africa are written in Europe over four months. No African state is represented.

keyDates.label: South African War begins
keyDates.why: Britain’s largest war between 1815 and 1914. Concentration camps kill about 28,000 Boer and at least 20,000 African civilians.

keyDates.label: Amritsar massacre
keyDates.why: Troops fire on a penned crowd; at least 379 killed by the official count, likely far more. The moment Indian moderates give up on the empire.

keyDates.label: Irish Free State established
keyDates.why: The first territory to leave the empire by force since America, and the first partition.

keyDates.label: Statute of Westminster
keyDates.why: Britain gives up the power to legislate for the dominions. Where independence "happens", if it happens on a day.

keyDates.label: Fall of Singapore
keyDates.why: 80,000 troops surrender. The claim that British power protected Asia does not survive it.

keyDates.label: Bengal famine
keyDates.why: Between 2.1 and 3 million dead in a province with food in it, under a government that kept exporting rice.

keyDates.label: India and Pakistan independent
keyDates.why: The empire loses four fifths of its subjects in one day. Partition displaces 12-18 million and kills between 200,000 and 2 million.

keyDates.label: Burma independent
keyDates.why: And leaves the Commonwealth, which almost nobody else does.

keyDates.label: Kenya emergency declared
keyDates.why: Eight years of detention camps: over 1,000 hanged, at least 80,000 detained, compensation finally paid by Britain in 2013.

keyDates.label: Suez landings
keyDates.why: Britain and France invade, the United States forces them out in a week. The end of Britain acting alone.

keyDates.label: Ghana independent
keyDates.why: The first sub-Saharan colony to go. Fifteen more African countries follow within four years.

keyDates.label: "Wind of change" speech
keyDates.why: Macmillan tells the South African parliament that African nationalism is a fact. Decolonisation accelerates.

keyDates.label: Rhodesian UDI
keyDates.why: A settler government declares independence rather than accept majority rule. Fifteen years of war follow.

keyDates.label: Withdrawal from East of Suez announced
keyDates.why: Britain says it will leave the Gulf and South-East Asia by 1971 because it cannot afford to stay.

keyDates.label: Argentina invades the Falklands
keyDates.why: The last colonial war Britain fought, and won: 649 Argentine, 255 British and 3 islander deaths.

keyDates.label: Hong Kong handed to China
keyDates.why: 6.5 million people transferred because a 99-year lease on the New Territories expired. The conventional end of the empire.

keyDates.label: ICJ advisory opinion on Chagos
keyDates.why: The court finds Britain’s detachment of the Chagos Archipelago unlawful. Decolonisation is not finished.

controlDegree.label: Claimed, not controlled
controlDegree.definition: On the map, but Britain gives no orders that are obeyed. The thirteen colonies between 1776 and 1783; a dominion after its own courts stopped taking appeals to London.

controlDegree.label: Influence only
controlDegree.definition: Britain shapes trade, debt or defence and nothing else.

controlDegree.label: Local government decides
controlDegree.definition: Ministers or a ruler on the spot govern; Britain holds reserve powers it rarely uses.

controlDegree.label: Shared or indirect
controlDegree.definition: A British official advises, supervises or vetoes; local structures do the day-to-day governing.

controlDegree.label: British administration, local law
controlDegree.definition: British officials govern, often through existing courts, chiefs or revenue systems.

controlDegree.label: Direct rule
controlDegree.definition: A British governor rules, with British law and no elected majority to stop him.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Settlement
acquisitionMechanism.definition: Settlers arrive and claim land as if it were empty. It rarely was: the legal doctrine of terra nullius was a claim about law, not about who lived there.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Conquest
acquisitionMechanism.definition: Taken by force from the people who held it. Say so plainly; "acquired" is a euphemism.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Chartered company
acquisitionMechanism.definition: A royal charter gives a private company a trade monopoly and the right to fortify, fight and govern. The East India Company, the Hudson’s Bay Company, the Royal Niger Company, the British South Africa Company.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Treaty cession
acquisitionMechanism.definition: Handed over in a treaty, usually by a defeated state, sometimes by a ruler who did not understand or did not control what he was signing away.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Purchase
acquisitionMechanism.definition: Bought for money. Rare, and the price is worth knowing: Britain paid Denmark for the Gold Coast forts in 1850 and the Netherlands for others in 1872.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Protectorate declared
acquisitionMechanism.definition: Britain announces protection, often after a treaty signed by a ruler with no power to sign it, and usually without conquest.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Lease
acquisitionMechanism.definition: Rented for a term of years from a state that keeps sovereignty. Weihaiwei, the New Territories.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Reorganisation of British territory
acquisitionMechanism.definition: No new land: existing British possessions are merged, split or re-labelled. Federations and unions belong here.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Transferred by a peace treaty
acquisitionMechanism.definition: Changed hands at the end of a war between European powers, with the inhabitants not consulted. Most of the Caribbean changed owner this way, some islands five or six times.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Mandate award
acquisitionMechanism.definition: Assigned by the League of Nations in 1920-22 from the wreck of the German and Ottoman empires.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Trusteeship award
acquisitionMechanism.definition: Assigned by the United Nations from 1946, with a duty to prepare the territory for independence.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Condominium agreement
acquisitionMechanism.definition: Two powers agree to govern jointly rather than fight over a place.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Military occupation
acquisitionMechanism.definition: Taken and held by armed force without a decision about its final status.

acquisitionMechanism.label: Informal influence
acquisitionMechanism.definition: No transfer of sovereignty at all: a loan, a gunboat, a treaty port, an adviser in the palace.

departureMechanism.label: Negotiated independence
departureMechanism.definition: Independence settled by conference and statute, usually after years of pressure that stopped short of war. The commonest exit after 1947.

departureMechanism.label: War of independence
departureMechanism.definition: Britain fought to keep it and lost, or fought and left. The United States, Ireland, and, argued either way, Aden and Cyprus.

departureMechanism.label: Insurgency, then negotiation
departureMechanism.definition: An armed campaign that Britain contained militarily but not politically, ending in a handover: Cyprus 1960, Kenya 1963, Malaya 1957.

departureMechanism.label: Partition
departureMechanism.definition: The territory is divided on the way out, usually along a line drawn in weeks. India and Pakistan 1947, Palestine 1948, Ireland 1921, Cyprus in effect after 1974.

departureMechanism.label: Transferred to another power
departureMechanism.definition: Handed to a different state rather than made independent: Heligoland to Germany 1890, Weihaiwei to China 1930, Hong Kong to China 1997.

departureMechanism.label: Lease expiry
departureMechanism.definition: The rental term ran out. Only Britain’s leases in China ended this way.

departureMechanism.label: Merged into a larger territory
departureMechanism.definition: It stopped existing as a separate territory by joining another. Often the empire did not leave that day: Nova Scotia joined Canada in 1867 and stayed British.

departureMechanism.label: Referendum
departureMechanism.definition: The inhabitants voted on their future. Newfoundland 1948, British Togoland 1956, the Northern Cameroons 1961.

departureMechanism.label: Never left
departureMechanism.definition: It is still British. Fourteen Overseas Territories, three Crown dependencies, and the Sovereign Base Areas on Cyprus.

datePrecision.label: Exact date
datePrecision.definition: Day, month and year are documented.

datePrecision.label: Month
datePrecision.definition: The month is known, the day is not.

datePrecision.label: Year
datePrecision.definition: The year is known, the day is not, or nothing happened on one day.

datePrecision.label: About
datePrecision.definition: Approximate. The sources disagree by a year or two.

datePrecision.label: Decade
datePrecision.definition: Only the decade can be defended.

datePrecision.label: Range
datePrecision.definition: It happened over a period, not at a moment.

datePrecision.label: Contested
datePrecision.definition: Historians actively disagree about the date, and the disagreement matters. The atlas shows the whole range and names who argues what: Canada 1867/1931/1982, Australia 1901/1942/1986.

datePrecision.label: Unknown
datePrecision.definition: We do not know, and the atlas says so rather than guessing.
